forces: Tenor soloist, mixed chorus, brass, timpani, harp and organ
performers: Michel Sénéchal, tenor; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; members of the Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
question: How does Boulanger make the return of the full choir feel larger than the opening?
intro: Brass and organ, without orchestral strings or woodwinds, give this short psalm its public, ringing character. A quieter tenor passage interrupts the proclamation before the full chorus expands it. Michel Sénéchal is the named soloist on this mono Everest recording.

cues.title: Brass without a string cushion
cues.text: The opening is built from trumpet and trombone chords, tuba and organ, with timpani joining the gesture. There are no orchestral strings or woodwinds anywhere in this score. Listen for the weight of the attacks and the space between them.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, nomenclature and printed p. 1: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: A Roman score
cues.text: The final page dates the work “Rome 1916.” This belongs to Boulanger’s second stay at the Villa Medici, after her 1913 Prix de Rome success; it is not a score written for the Everest album issued in 1960.

cues.title: The soloist’s smaller surroundings
cues.text: The central tenor passage replaces the opening’s massed attack with a more intimate combination: muted horns, harp and organ. Listen for how the space around one voice changes the scale of the psalm without changing its basic ensemble.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 6–7, figure 3, Un peu moins vite: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-24.txt: the strong 1:12 boundary and quieter, darker 1:15–1:30 windows place the central contrast approximately. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dedication to Griset
cues.text: The score is dedicated to Jules Griset, a choral conductor. Its public voice is therefore not only a modern listener’s impression: the work has a specific connection with French choral life.
cues.evidence: The dedication is also printed on score p. 1: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1146.html

cues.title: The whole choir opens out
cues.text: The later proclamation uses all four choral groups, not just the lower voices heard in the opening design. Returning brass gestures now support a wider vocal range. Compare that enlargement with the tenor passage’s more private scale.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 8–9, Au mouvement: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-24.txt: the increase in brightness near 2:10 and sustained stronger level after it locate the larger concluding span approximately. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nadia behind the recording
cues.text: The original sleeve says that the recording was made under Nadia Boulanger’s direction. It separately names Igor Markevitch as conductor. Those are different credits: Nadia’s supervision is not a licence to replace Markevitch on the performing roster.
cues.evidence: Original LPBR 6059 insert header and credits. https://i.discogs.com/XrNcaeuOsiqmWirxmPgDAtlexW1ImUbc9UpE5Aw4kkg/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:600/w:592/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MDk5/Ny02MDQ1LmpwZWc.jpeg

cues.title: A decisive final release
cues.text: The force of the closing passage gives way rapidly to the remaining resonance. Let the final sound finish: this is the end of an independent psalm, not a transition into a second movement.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-24.txt, the level falls from the strong late passage to −13.8 dB at 3:25 and −24.3 dB at 3:30; total duration 3:30.1 Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

transitions.title: Brass weight yields to muted horns
transitions.how: The opening’s lower-voice declamation and brass punctuation make room for a solo tenor. At figure 3, “Un peu moins vite” relaxes the motion; muted horns exchange a small figure above harp and organ. The continuous organ part bridges the change, while reduced brass weight and a single vocal line turn proclamation into a more intimate utterance.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 5–7, figure 3: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-24.txt: novelty peaks at 1:12; the quieter 1:15–1:30 stretch supplies the broad anchor. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: The choir widens the proclamation
transitions.how: After the solo passage, lower voices broaden the line at “Plus lent.” Harp motion and sustained brass lead to “Au mouvement,” where sopranos and altos join the renewed proclamation. Returning brass rhythms connect it to the opening, but the now-complete choir enlarges the register and weight. This is an expansion through scoring, not a newly introduced string orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 7–9, Plus lent through Au mouvement: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf. composer.epithet: Her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.
facts: Daughter of Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger; younger sister of the composer, conductor and teacher Nadia Boulanger
Paris Conservatoire; composition with Paul Vidal, with extensive musical support from Nadia
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, 1913
Songs, choral works, orchestral and chamber pieces; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
Lili Boulanger grew up in a Paris household where composition, singing and teaching were family work. Her father Ernest had won the Prix de Rome in 1835 and taught singing at the Conservatoire; her mother Raïssa had been his pupil. Nadia, born in 1887, was already receiving serious musical training when Lili was small. Lili learned piano and several other instruments and accompanied her sister into Conservatoire classes. Recurrent illness interrupted her education from childhood. The resulting timetable was irregular, but the musical environment was exceptionally well supplied with teachers, performers and scores.

Nadia was an early mentor and practical support; Lili’s formal composition teacher at the Conservatoire was Paul Vidal. Their training included fugue, harmony and the cantata, extending well beyond the short piano pieces through which women composers were often permitted a public identity. In 1912 illness forced Lili to withdraw from the final stage of the Prix de Rome. She returned in 1913 and won the Premier Grand Prix with Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive that composition prize. She was nineteen. Nadia had won a second prize in 1908.
